resources.string: Choose names that describe intent. Clear names make Kotlin code easier to review and reduce the need for explanatory comments.
Start with val and immutable collections. Introduce mutation only when the state truly needs to change.
Give each composable one visual responsibility. Small composables are easier to preview, test, and reuse.
Accept a Modifier parameter on reusable composables and apply it to the outermost layout so callers control placement.
Build logs often contain follow-up failures. Start with the first meaningful compiler or resource error and fix it before chasing the rest.
Move calculations into plain Kotlin functions and cover boundary values with fast unit tests.
Provide a concise content description when an image conveys information. Use null when the image is purely decorative.
Use data classes for the exact information a screen needs. Strong models make rendering code predictable.
LazyColumn and LazyVerticalGrid compose only visible items, which keeps long lists responsive.
Stable keys help Compose preserve item state and animate changes correctly when a list is reordered.
Write down the shortest sequence that triggers a bug. A reliable reproduction turns guessing into verification.
Interactive controls should be easy to reach and large enough to activate comfortably, even when their icon is small.
Move state to the lowest common owner that needs to read or change it, then pass values and events down.
Use nullable types only when absence is a valid state, and make the fallback behavior visible in the code.
For ranges and limits, test the value below, at, and above the boundary. These cases catch many off-by-one errors.
Use the debugger and logs to inspect the data that produced the UI instead of changing layout code blindly.
Text and icons need enough contrast in both light and dark themes. Do not rely on color alone to communicate status.
Create previews for light, dark, large text, empty data, and long content so layout problems appear early.
Store user-facing text, dimensions, colors, and images in resources so they can be localized and reused.
Avoid real clocks, random values, and network calls in unit tests. Inject controllable inputs instead.
Filter by application process and a consistent tag so the useful signal is not buried in device noise.
Let text wrap and avoid fixed-height text containers. Test the screen with a larger system font scale.
Motion should explain a state change. Keep animations short, interruptible, and connected to the action the user took.
Extract a helper when a function mixes several levels of detail. A short function is easier to name and verify.
Compose UI tests should locate controls by visible text, role, or content description instead of screen coordinates.
Place breakpoints where data changes or decisions branch. Too many breakpoints make the important transition harder to see.
Try the screen with TalkBack or another accessibility service to discover missing labels and confusing focus order.
Choose colors and typography through MaterialTheme roles so components remain coherent across light and dark modes.
A debug build can hide release-only problems. Compile the release variant before considering the project complete.
Run the tests, inspect the final diff, document what you learned, and keep a small list of improvements for the next app.
